> Destination Dispatch [...] are in general worseI wonder if this is an artifact of how the author used random destinations.  I worked in a building that used Destination Dispatch, and the common travel pattern seemed to be:- Everyone who is not on the ground floor generally want to go to the ground floor.- People who are on the ground floor generally travel in large groups to the same destination.This happens because people who worked on the same floor often leave for lunch at the same time, and return at the same time to the same floor.  Destination Dispatch helps in this case because it's batching large groups of people with the same destination.reply

This is case where you need to make sure your test data reflects real-world usage or you end up optimizing for the wrong thing.Ideally a new elevator installation would have a trial period where they record usage and then run it through a simulator like this to determine the optimal strategy for that particular building. The way you push their buttons, and how they push yours.The simplest elevator algorithm is called SCAN and was patented in 1961. The elevator starts at the lobby and goes all the way to the top floor before reversing and coming back down. It picks up and drops off anybody on the way.Most of the time you don't actually need to go to the TOP floor. If the elevator goes only as high as requested before reversing, the algorithm is called the LOOK algorithm. This is the algorithm most people know and expect.Here's where the mystery begins. As it happens, I recently re-read The Stranger -- the last time was in 2006, so it was essentially fresh.The first half of the short book is easily on-par with any of the great masterpieces of literature.  It was written in a direct, vivid, gripping, and yet somehow languorous style -- something almost paradoxical.  It was also very attuned to the aesthetics and flow of the outside world, but inattentive to the narrator's inner life -- insensitive and, in a sense, essentially masculine in a non-performative way.  As a purely aesthetic work, it is truly excellent.The second half falls apart catastrophically.  The key scenario, the book's turning point, is contrived almost beyond belief.  The trial is a farce on several distinct levels -- you can criticize it from almost any perspective, and you'd be right.  (There's a well-known Orientalist critique which is just the tip of the iceberg.)  And the close of the book brings with it a number of unreliable narrator problems, which make the book as difficult to resolve as time-travel fiction.My impression was that it worked wonderfully as pure prose, and that Camus should probably have written travel journals a la Gerard Nerval.  As philosophy, though, it was hopelessly muddled, badly contrived, and confused.reply

At least from my perspective, the trial is meant to be contrived and a farce. From Meursault's perspective (which I agree that he can be an unreliable narrator) everything happening around him is inconsequential; he reflects that death-even of someone so "close" to him as his mother-doesn't matter as the end would always come. Meursault is on trial for his disposition, rather than the actual murder. The prosecution argues that Meursault is guilty due to his aloofness rather than any discussion of the murder (the defense openly questions whether Meursault is on trial for the murder of the arab or the murder of his mother!). At least for me, this difference was what _The Stranger_ was about; this inherent clash between indifference and the human rejection of the "gentle indifference of the universe". The fact that Meursault's unreliable narrator aspect comes about of the confrontation between the priest(?) and himself makes me think that Meursault too was hiding under this coating of lucidity, where he (and others who pretend to be stoics in the face of the absurd) will eventually break down. I reccomend reading _The Myth of Sisyphus_, especially the third and fourth parts, for Camus' explanation of the absurd hero.Also, could you link the critiques? They sound interesting and I'd like to read them.reply

The problem as I see it is in the fact that the book describes the world very naturalistically.  The first half of the book is basically Proust, if Proust were less introspective and didn't care to inflate his word count.  It's actually rare to find a book where the events of day-to-day life -- running to catch a tram, or spending a lazy Sunday afternoon on one's balcony -- are relayed with such clarity and directness.Then the murder happens -- which was a highly contrived and even quite ridiculous scenario, in that (a) Mersault's party was quite literally being stalked by an armed gang, (b) Mersault separated himself from the pack and was menaced by one of his stalkers, who was armed with a knife, (c) the naked knife was in the man's hand, as that man was blocking Mersault's path, (d) there were no witnesses, and (e) Mersault was a Frenchman in colonial French Algeria.Not 1 in 10000 times does that go to court for murder, and not 1 in 1000000 times does it result in the death penalty.But, anyway, back to my point:  The minute the murder happens, we're yanked out of the naturalistic world and thrust directly into the world of Kafka's The Trial.  Nothing makes sense any longer.  What once was so true-to-life becomes something akin to the hallucinatory descent of divine justice -- a bad trip, a fever dream.  "Yeah, you're off to the guillotine because you didn't cry at your mom's funeral.  What kind of monster are you?"  The most parsimonious interpretation is that the narrator has simply lost his mind.Don't even get me started on the fact that every reviewer thinks that Mersault was executed, when that never actually happens in the book, and would result in him not being able to write the book in the first place.  (Further confused by the variety of tenses used in the construction of the prose.)  The book, which is written something like a memoir, ends with his appeal still pending, and the prison chaplain "sure of its success."As to the critiques, the Orientalist one is in Edward Said's "Culture and Imperialism" but I don't think that the full version is online.  As I recall, it basically concerned point (e) above, and noted that the trial would not have happened -- so the notion of the trial may be a sort of cope.reply

It’s been a while, but I recall finding The Plague more compelling than The Stranger.While I agree with Camus’s philosophical points about the absurdity of existence and the indifference of the universe, within the scope of our tiny little lives there is morality and meaning.  Taking action to address the suffering caused by an epidemic is meaningful. So are the deaths of an Arab or one’s mother, and the premise that a human would be so alienated that they would feel nothing at them is unconvincing, even if the universe doesn’t care.There was an essay in The Guardian a couple days ago on a related topic, positing that the essence of the self is the biological body including the brain, rather than the isolated mind. https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2026/jul/30/alive-...reply

title: Progressive Web Components (arielsalminen.com)
comments: I think it's better to think of "Web components" as "Custom Elements" they really aren't components in the way you think of components in other frameworks (which on the web introduced them first), and I think most of the dissatisfaction with them comes from trying pretend they're an alternative as they just aren't. Components in almost every other framework are efficient (efficient rendering runtime) and expressive (the ability not to have a root element but instead a frag, or context APIs etc) in ways that web components never will be, which makes them unappealing.But when you think of them as a suite of APIs to define custom elements, that can coexist with your framework components, this delimma goes away.I do think it's a-shame that modern frameworks don't better support shadow dom and local styles, and local events. Understandably I also get why they also don't see that as a good use of their time either, it adds complexity to the runtimes, they need to observe events at multiple root nodes.Besides the cost of implementation and commitment to additional complexity, assuming that was a nonissue, with the exception of those otherwise legitimate reasons, there's no technical limitation that prevents React from supporting shadow roots for arbitrary custom element. I made a proof of concept of this myself seems to work quite nicely with a stylesheet loader hook (which ensured it was loaded once and there was a shared sheet between all instances of the same element), but I had to start observing events in each elements shadow root.reply

One fun thing I did once is use the custom elements API to make a custom tag <element-template>. When the page sees <element-template tag=what-name></element-template>, it looks inside, finds any <template></template> <script></script> and <style></style> tags, and builds a new custom element with that tag name and all the powers. Cool but not incredibly simple.Another amazing trick is to put a mutation observer on the page to detect <template> tags as they're created. (template tags parse the HTML within but don't actually create it on the page). Once the observer finds a template tag it can upgrade them to have new powers, like replacing the contents of other tags. There are ways to tame web components and make them very easy to use.reply

first_paragraph: I’ve worked with web components for nearly a decade and built various enterprise-scale design systems with them. While I love what they offer on paper, the same pain points keep coming back:Layout shifts, flash of unstyled content, poor server-side rendering support, too much reliance on client side JavaScript, doesn't play well with frame­works like React Server Components, accessibility issues, and so on…Despite all of this, I still think web components are a great foundation for a design system. No other approach gives you true cross-framework portability built on what the web platform already provides. The problem isn’t necessarily the model itself, it’s how we’ve been building them.This is how I ended up creating Elena, a library that I’m open sourcing today. Slight hardware revisions of adapters/switches, which if you are lucky can be differentiated by manufacture date or serial number sequence, will not recognize known good modules, and if they do you then have to actually test if they can establish link, then let them burn for 24+ hours to see if they can maintain it without dropping (often, because of forward error correction, you will not start to see flapping until enough correctable errors have accumulated and the buffer overflows). Then there are firmware updates where this process must then be repeated.You would think with how expensive all of this shit is you would simply be able to buy the officially listed as compatible components but my experience with them has been that a shotgun approach is best for your sanity and deadlines, buying sample kits of each module and trying them all, and then once you find the ones that play nice, buying as many of them as is reasonable and testing all of them.If I had a dollar every time two modules from the same brand, that came in the same box, from the same production run, did not work with one another, I would be able to test your theory for free.
